screens.title: Post-Deployment Monitoring & Analytics (Basic)
screens.subtitle: Collect crash reports, send custom events, and turn player telemetry into development priorities.

narration.text: Deploying a game is the start of a learning cycle, not the finish line. In this lesson you will learn why monitoring deployed builds matters, how Unity Cloud Diagnostics catches crashes and exceptions, and how Unity Analytics records gameplay events so you can make data-driven updates. You will see a practical example of sending custom events from C# and a small lab that simulates an error, so you can verify reporting in a development build. We will also cover the types of information those services provide — stack traces, device metadata, event parameters — and how that information helps you prioritize fixes and design changes. Finally, we discuss privacy considerations so your telemetry respects player rights. By the end you will be able to enable both services, add a simple custom event to your code, run a development build to surface errors, and read the basic dashboards to find problems and opportunities. Think about one actionable metric you would want to track for your own game as you follow along.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Monitoring and analytics turn player activity and crashes into actionable development priorities, enabling iterative improvements after release.

screens.title: Why Post-Deployment Monitoring Matters
screens.subtitle: From single crashes to long-term design insight

narration.text: Post-deployment monitoring is the ongoing process of collecting error and usage data after a build reaches players. The key claim is that many issues only appear at scale or on particular hardware combinations, so telemetry lets you observe real-world behavior and prioritize effort where it matters most. For example, a crash that affects 2 percent of sessions on an older G P U model should be prioritized differently than a UI button that confused 20 percent of new players. Monitoring gives you both stability signals, like crash frequency and stack traces, and behavioral signals, like session length and item usage. A common misconception is thinking telemetry replaces testing; it does not. Testing tries to prevent problems, while monitoring discovers ones you didn't catch. Practically, you will use this data to decide whether to ship a hotfix, roll back a build, or redesign a mechanic. In this lesson we also outline the feedback loop that turns raw data into prioritized tasks: collect, group, analyze, act, and measure the result. As a reflection, think which single metric would most impact your game's survival if you could improve it by 10 percent.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Monitoring captures stability and behavior in the wild so you can prioritize fixes and design changes based on real player data.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Why Monitoring Matters
What is post-deployment monitoring?
Ongoing collection of crash, exception and user behavior data from deployed builds.
Practical benefit
Prioritize high-impact fixes by combining crash frequency and player reach data.
Misconception
Monitoring does not replace QA. It complements testing by revealing issues that only appear at scale or on specific devices.
Key Takeaway

Monitoring provides the evidence you need to make focused, high-impact development decisions after release.

Concrete example
If a crash cluster shows a stack trace linked to a rendering call on a specific GPU, you may choose to disable an optional shader for that device class until a fix ships.
Steps to form a feedback loop:
  • Collect telemetry automatically from deployed builds.
  • Group similar crashes and view device statistics.
  • Analyze player behavior and event funnels for design issues.
  • Prioritize fixes or content changes and deploy an update.
  • Measure the effect of changes through new telemetry.
Reflection prompt
Which single metric, if improved by ten percent, would most increase your game’s retention or stability?

screens.title: Enable Unity Cloud Diagnostics
screens.subtitle: Quick steps to get crash and exception reporting turned on

narration.text: Unity Cloud Diagnostics collects crashes, unhandled exceptions, and error trends from deployed builds. Enabling it is a short process inside the Unity Editor and then you will rely on the Dashboard to inspect results. The steps are: open the Services window, link your project to an organization if needed, enable Cloud Diagnostics, and ensure crash and exception reporting is checked. A common error is assuming reporting is active across all builds; remember that development or build settings may affect reporting, and you should verify in a development build with diagnostics enabled. After enabling, expect automatic grouping of similar crashes and stack traces tied to device metadata. Practically, once crash reports arrive you will look at stack traces, device models, OS versions, and frequency to decide whether an issue is platform-specific or widespread. If you do not see data, check that the build has networking enabled and that it is a development build if you rely on extra diagnostic symbols. This process turns silent failures into actionable issues you can triage. screens.title: Unity Cloud Diagnostics: What It Reports
screens.subtitle: Crash reports, exceptions, error groups, and device metadata

narration.text: Unity Cloud Diagnostics gathers several key artifacts from crashes and exceptions. A crash report usually includes a stack trace pointing to the chain of function calls that led to the crash, plus device metadata such as model and OS version. Exceptions that do not crash the game are still valuable; they reveal error conditions you may want to handle or log differently. Cloud Diagnostics groups similar errors so you can see which problems affect many players versus isolated cases. The combination of stack traces and device breakdown helps you decide whether a fix is platform-specific, driver-related, or an underlying code bug. A frequent mistake is overreacting to a single report without checking frequency and device context. Instead, use groups and frequency to estimate impact. In practice, you will use this information to assign priority, reproduce the issue on similar hardware if possible, and ship a targeted fix. Always pair the crash data with any related analytics events that might indicate what the player was doing before the crash. narration.text: Unity Analytics gives you pre-built reports and the ability to send custom events for richer insights. To enable analytics, open the Services window and toggle Analytics on, then accept any terms required. On the Dashboard you'll find basic reports for daily active users, session length, and retention. Those pre-built views are useful for an initial health check: watch session length trends after a major update or check if daily active users fall after an event. However, pre-built reports have limits; the real power comes from custom events that capture domain-specific actions like 'LevelCompleted' or 'ItemUsed'. A common pitfall is relying only on aggregate metrics without segmenting players by device, region, or acquisition source. Use segments and custom event parameters to answer targeted questions: are new players dropping during the tutorial, or do paying players behave differently? Practically, enable analytics, let it collect baseline metrics, then plan a small set of custom events that answer the most important design questions for your game. Design checklist for events:
  • Will this event answer a specific design question?
  • What parameters provide context for the event?
  • Can the event be triggered frequently without over-reporting?

screens.title: Custom Events in C#: Structure and Parameters
screens.subtitle: How to design and send meaningful events from scripts

narration.text: Custom events are simple developer-defined messages with optional key-value parameters that provide context. Their structure is an event name and a dictionary of parameters. When designing events, choose a clear naming convention, keep parameter keys consistent, and include only the context you need. For example, 'LevelCompleted' with parameters for level_name and time_taken gives you a completion signal plus performance context. A common error is logging player identifiers when not necessary; prefer anonymous IDs or only collect personal data with consent. The provided GameAnalyticsManager script demonstrates a pattern: a singleton manager with methods for ReportLevelCompleted and ReportItemUsed that call Analytics. CustomEvent with a dictionary. This keeps analytics code centralized and makes it easier to change event names or add parameters later. In practice, group event definitions in one place, document each parameter, and avoid sending high-cardinality values that make segmentation noisy. Think about which three events would answer your most pressing design questions before you add code. content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Designing Custom Events
Event anatomy
An event name plus a dictionary of parameters provides context for segmentation and funnels.
Design rules
  • Use consistent, descriptive event names like LevelCompleted or ItemUsed.
  • Keep parameter keys consistent and low-cardinality where possible.
  • Centralize event sending in a manager script for maintainability.
Key Takeaway

Well-designed events answer specific design questions and remain stable as your project grows.

Example code (visual only)
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.Analytics;
using System.Collections.Generic;

public class GameAnalyticsManager : MonoBehaviour
{
    public static GameAnalyticsManager Instance { get; private set; }

    void Awake()
    {
        if (Instance != null && Instance != this) Destroy(gameObject);
        else Instance = this;
    }

    public void ReportLevelCompleted(string levelName, float timeTaken)
    {
        Analytics.CustomEvent("LevelCompleted", new Dictionary<string, object> {
            { "level_name", levelName },
            { "time_taken_seconds", timeTaken }
        });
    }
}
Centralize events so you can change names or parameters without hunting through many scripts.

screens.title: Lab: AnalyticsTest — Send Events and Simulate an Error

narration.text: This lab uses a small script that demonstrates both sending custom events and simulating an error for Cloud Diagnostics. The script sends a GameStarted event on Start with a session identifier and device model. In Update it sends a PlayerUsedAbility event when you press a key, and simulates a NullReferenceException when you press another key. Run these steps: attach the script to an empty GameObject, build as a development build with networking, run the build and press the event key a few times, then trigger the simulated exception so a crash or exception is recorded. A common misconception is that pressing keys in the Editor will always produce dashboard results; make sure you run the built player if you expect Cloud Diagnostics data. After a few minutes, check the Dashboard for the GameStarted and PlayerUsedAbility events and for the exception entry. This exercise shows both the analytics event flow and how Cloud Diagnostics captures unexpected runtime errors. Lab steps

  2. Enable Analytics and Cloud Diagnostics in Services.
  3. Build a development build with networking enabled.
  4. Run the built player, press the event key several times, then press the crash key.
  5. Wait and verify events and the exception on the Dashboard.
Checklist

Confirm service toggles, build settings, and that the built player can reach the network for reporting.

Example script (visual)
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.Analytics;
using System.Collections.Generic;

public class AnalyticsTest : MonoBehaviour
{
    void Start()
    {
        Analytics.CustomEvent("GameStarted", new Dictionary
        {
            { "session_id", System.Guid.NewGuid().ToString() },
            { "device_model", SystemInfo.deviceModel }
        });
    }

    void Update()
    {
        if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.E))
        {
            Analytics.CustomEvent("PlayerUsedAbility", new Dictionary
            {
                { "ability_name", "Dash" },
                { "cooldown_remaining", 5.0f }
            });
        }

        if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.C))
        {
            Debug.LogError("Simulating a critical error!");
            string nullRef = null;
            Debug.Log(nullRef.Length); // This will cause a NullReferenceException
        }
    }
}
Run the steps and allow a few minutes for the Dashboard to process and display events and exceptions.

A common trap is neglecting to wait for processing. Data pipelines may delay events and crash grouping for several minutes, so allow a small window before concluding the pipeline failed. This build-and-verify practice keeps your monitoring confidence high before production releases. screens.title: Crash Data vs Analytics Events
screens.subtitle: How stability signals and behavior signals complement each other

narration.text: Crash data and analytics events serve different but complementary roles. Crash data, captured by Cloud Diagnostics, tells you where the program failed and on which devices. It's a stability signal that often includes a stack trace and frequency metrics. Analytics events, recorded by Unity Analytics, tell you what players did — the flow they followed, items they used, and how long they spent. Combining both provides context: a crash that occurs after a specific event can be tied to the player action that preceded it. For example, if a crash group spikes whenever many players use a new ability, analytics can point to that ability as the likely trigger, while the crash stack trace pinpoints the failing code. A common misconception is treating them as interchangeable; they are not. Use crash data to fix stability issues and analytics to understand behavior, funnels, and how players reach error states. In practice, link events to crashes where possible to shorten the time to root cause and to avoid guessing about player flows that led to failures. Crash Data vs Analytics Events means use crash data to locate errors and analytics events to understand the player actions that lead to those errors.. In practical terms, how stability signals and behavior signals complement each other. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Crash Data (Cloud Diagnostics)
Stability-focused, includes stack traces, device metadata, and grouped errors for triage.
  • Use for pinpointing failing code and platform-specific bugs.
  • Prioritize by frequency and affected user base.
Analytics Events (Unity Analytics)
Behavior-focused, records actions and parameters so you can analyze progression and funnels.
  • Use for understanding player paths and measuring the impact of design changes.
  • Segment by parameters to find which players see high crash rates or drop off.
Combined workflow
When a crash spikes, check recent analytics funnels to see what players were doing, then use stack traces to fix the code. This reduces guesswork and speeds resolution.

screens.title: Privacy, Data Minimization & Ethical Considerations
screens.subtitle: Respect player privacy while collecting useful data

narration.text: When instrumenting analytics you must be mindful of privacy and legal requirements. Collect only data that is necessary to improve gameplay or stability. Avoid personally identifiable information unless you have a clear legal basis and explicit player consent. Examples of unnecessary data include raw device owner names or full contact details. Instead, use anonymous identifiers or aggregated metrics that allow segmentation without exposing players. Another common pitfall is over-instrumentation: logging every possible action can create noise and increase storage and analysis cost. A better approach is to design a compact set of events that answer clear questions about retention, progression, or monetization. Also document your data policies for players and internal teams so everyone understands what is collected and why. Finally, when you export data or share it with third parties, ensure it is appropriately anonymized and only includes fields required for the task. Privacy, Data Minimization & Ethical Considerations means collect minimal, necessary telemetry; prefer anonymous identifiers and explicit consent for any personal data.. In practical terms, respect player privacy while collecting useful data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Three essential ideas to keep in mind

narration.text: These three core concepts summarize the practical parts of post-deployment monitoring. First, Post-Deployment Monitoring is the practice of observing stability and behavior in released builds; it informs priorities that testing cannot reveal at scale. Second, Unity Cloud Diagnostics is the stability tool that gathers crash reports and exceptions with stack traces and device data so you can triage platform-specific failures. Third, Unity Analytics captures gameplay events and session metrics; when extended with custom events and parameters, it answers specific design questions about progression and engagement. Keep these concepts in mind as a lightweight checklist when you enable services, design events, or prioritize fixes: check stability, measure behavior, and ensure data supports an actionable feedback loop. Post-Deployment Monitoring

Unity Cloud Diagnostics

Unity Analytics

Takeaway
Use diagnostics for stability and analytics for behavior, and connect them to shorten time to resolution and guide design choices.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 2
screens.subtitle: Three practical reminders for your workflow

narration.text: Three practical reminders to carry forward: first, centralize your analytics calls in a manager script so you can change event names or parameters without editing many files. Second, design a small set of high-value events before adding instrumentation; this reduces noise and keeps dashboards actionable. Third, respect privacy: avoid unnecessary personal identifiers and document what you collect. Together these practices make your telemetry useful, maintainable, and ethically sound. When you leave this lesson, draft the three events you will implement first and one simulated crash you will use to validate diagnostics. That small preparation saves time and prevents noisy telemetry that does not support decisions.
